young.html: Martin Heidegger (say HY-deg-er) was a German philosopher who asked one of the biggest questions there is: why is there something, rather than nothing at all?

Scientists study things: rocks, plants, stars, people. Heidegger noticed that every science studies some kind of thing, and nothing else. But what about that "nothing"? Can we even think about it? He thought certain moments, like a strange quiet feeling when everything seems far away, make us wonder at the fact that anything exists at all.

young.cap: Tap the rings: each science studies one region of what exists; Heidegger asks about all of it at once, and about the nothing around it.

young.html: Wonder walk. Go outside for five minutes without talking. Look at a tree, a cloud, a stone. Instead of asking "what is it?", ask "isn't it strange that it is there at all?" Talk afterward about how that felt.

full.html: Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) studied with Edmund Husserl, the founder of phenomenology, and made his name with Being and Time (1927). What Is Metaphysics? is the lecture he gave on July 24, 1929, when he took over Husserl's chair at the University of Freiburg. He later added a Postscript (1943) and an Introduction (1949).

No excerpts here. The lecture was first translated into English in 1949, so no English version is in the public domain in the U.S. This lesson describes it in our own words. Several translations are in libraries.

Heidegger starts with the university itself. Its many sciences, physics, biology, history and the rest, each study some region of beings (things that are), and nothing beyond it. Science says: we study beings, and nothing else. Then Heidegger asks: what about this nothing that science sets aside?

Logic cannot answer, he argues, because to think of "the nothing" seems to turn it into a something. But we do not meet the nothing first by thinking. We meet it in certain moods. In deep boredom, beings as a whole fall into a strange sameness. In what he calls anxiety (Angst), a mood with no particular object, everything seems to slip away from us, and we are left facing the bare fact that there is something at all.

full.html: From that experience Heidegger draws his conclusion: human existence is always "held out into the nothing," and that is why we can ask about beings as a whole, which is what metaphysics does. The lecture ends with the old question the philosopher Leibniz had asked two centuries before: why are there beings at all, rather than nothing?

The lecture became a classic of 20th-century "continental" philosophy, and its themes of mood, anxiety and the question of being shaped existentialism, theology and literary theory. It also became the most famous target of the logical positivists. In 1932 Rudolf Carnap took sentences from it, such as one that turns the word "nothing" into a verb, as his prime examples of statements that look meaningful but, he argued, say nothing that could be true or false. Heidegger's defenders reply that he was pointing to something language struggles to say, not making a claim of logic. Any account of Heidegger must also note that he joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and served for a year as rector of Freiburg under the regime; private notebooks published in 2014 contain antisemitic passages. Scholars still debate how far his politics affected his philosophy.
Thinking Heidegger meant that nothing is a kind of thing, or that he wanted people to feel anxious. He used moods as clues to what it means to exist at all.

items: Aristotle's Metaphysics called first philosophy the study of being as being; Heidegger thought the tradition since then had forgotten to ask what "being" means.
Leibniz asked "why is there something rather than nothing?"; Heidegger called it the fundamental question.
Kierkegaard, in the 19th-century rungs, wrote about anxiety as a mood that reveals freedom; Heidegger knew his work.
Wittgenstein, two rungs on, thought many such questions arise when language "goes on holiday"; compare Carnap's reply.
Beckett's Waiting for Godot, in the literature rungs, stages people facing emptiness with jokes and waiting.
Why is there anything at all?
Can a feeling teach us something true about the world?
Are there questions science cannot ask, or are they not real questions?
How should we read a great thinker who did wrong things?

questions: Why is there something rather than nothing? Does the question have an answer?
Have you ever had a quiet moment when the world seemed strange? What was it like?
Is it possible to think about "nothing"? Try, and say what happens.
Carnap said some philosophical sentences are meaningless. How would you decide whether a sentence means anything?
Heidegger joined the Nazi Party. Should that change how we read his books? Why or why not?
care: The lecture discusses anxiety and nothingness as philosophical themes, and the lesson notes Heidegger's Nazi Party membership factually. Suitable for older readers; young readers can do the wonder walk.
